title: A small asteroid turned out to have a moon, and the moon is two rocks stuck together

cover.alt: Black space with a small, sunlit, lumpy asteroid near the centre and a tiny speck of a second rock to its left.

body: On 1 November 2023, NASA’s Lucy spacecraft flew past **Dinkinesh**, a main-belt asteroid only about 790 m across, at 4.5 km/s and 425 km away. The visit was meant to test Lucy’s autonomous tracking before its real targets, the Trojan asteroids that share Jupiter’s orbit. Instead it found surprises: Dinkinesh has a small moon, now named **Selam**, and as Lucy swung past, the moon turned out to be two rocks touching each other, each about 220 m wide. Selam is the first known contact binary orbiting an asteroid.

slides.alt: Time-lapse of real spacecraft images on black: a lumpy grey asteroid grows from a small shape to fill much of the frame, with a smaller rock beside it at left, then shrinks again; afterwards its little moon shows up at right as two blobs side by side.
slides.caption: Time-lapse of Lucy’s images, 1 November 2023: Dinkinesh grows as the probe closes in, with its moon Selam beside it, then shrinks away. From this side, Selam shows two lobes.

slides.prompt: Dinkinesh is the Amharic name of the famous Lucy fossil found in Ethiopia. What does it mean?
slides.detail: Its moon is named Selam, Amharic for ‘peace’, after another fossil from Ethiopia: a three-year-old Australopithecus afarensis.

slides.label: Lucy’s speed past Dinkinesh, about 16,000 km/h
slides.text: At closest approach, at 16:54 UTC, it was 425 km from the asteroid, and Lucy had to keep its cameras pointed at the target on its own.

slides.question: Why did Lucy fly past Dinkinesh at all?
options: To use its gravity for a boost
slides.explanation: The flyby, announced in January 2023, was a rehearsal of Lucy’s autonomous tracking before its main targets: the Trojan asteroids that lead and trail Jupiter.
